title: Currency, paper and textile: three industries, three federations
author: Editorial Desk
summary: The Currency and Coins, Kagaz Udyog and Vastrodyog federations.
body:
Most people know the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh through its big rallies and its meetings with ministers. Less visible is the structure underneath: a set of industry-wise federations, each speaking for workers in one trade. Three of them, in currency and coins, paper and textiles, show how different those worlds can be, even though all three are bound by one organisation and one motto.

## How the federation system works

BMS is built in two directions at once. Geographically it has State units, and by industry it has All India federations, usually called a *Mahasangh*. The federations page on the BMS website lists **38** such bodies, from Anganwadi, construction, cement and sugar to railways, ports, banks, plantations and defence. A press report in August 2026 spoke of 42 industrial federations, so the exact count depends on how affiliates are grouped; this post uses the list published on the BMS site. An older pamphlet from the V.V. Giri National Labour Institute described 32 federations, which shows how the structure has grown over the years.

The logic is simple. A worker in a mint and a worker in a textile mill have different employers, different laws, different wage settlements and different dangers. A single general union cannot negotiate all of that well. A federation can collect the specific problems of one industry and carry them to the right ministry.

## Currency and coins

The **Bharatiya Currency and Coins Karamchari Mahasangh** is number 12 on the BMS list. The industry it points to is a small, specialised one. The Security Printing and Minting Corporation of India, a company wholly owned by the Ministry of Finance, was created in 2006 by bringing together the government's currency presses, security presses, paper mill and mints. It runs nine units: two currency note presses (Nashik and Dewas), two security presses (Nashik and Hyderabad), four India Government Mints (Mumbai, Kolkata, Hyderabad and Noida) and a security paper mill at Narmadapuram in Madhya Pradesh, which dates from 1968. Public sources put its workforce at 5,752 in 2024.

That is a very small number against BMS's overall claim of nearly ten million members, but the work matters out of proportion to its size. Every banknote and many coins in the country come from such units. Security, skill and secrecy mark the job. The issues this federation raises, such as wage structures, promotions and safety on machines and in print halls, are the kind that arise wherever skilled work is done inside a government corporation after a restructuring.

## Paper

The **Bharatiya Kagaz Udyog Karamchari Mahasangh** is number 15 on the list. Paper is an old, scattered industry. A trade report in PrintWeek, citing the Indian Paper Manufacturers Association, said that only about 550 of roughly 850 to 900 paper mills were operating. The reasons it gave were scarcity of raw material, competition from imports and rising costs, with competition from ASEAN countries also mentioned. The report carries no date and no job-loss figure, so it should be read as an indicator of stress rather than a precise count.

For workers, a mill that shuts is rarely a clean event. Paper mills are often the main employer in a small town. When one stops, the loss reaches contract workers, wood and bamboo suppliers and transporters as well as the permanent staff. This is why a paper federation spends much of its energy on questions of closure, retrenchment compensation and the dues of workers after a mill stops, and why the new Industrial Relations Code, with its rules on closure and retrenchment, is of direct interest to it.

## Textiles

The **Bharatiya Vastrodyog Karmachari Mahasangh** is number 26, and a related body, the **Bharatiya Jute Mazdoor Mahasangh**, is number 14. Textiles is the largest of the three industries by far. In a written reply to the Lok Sabha in December 2022, the Government's Ministry of Textiles estimated direct employment in the sector at 45 million. The fourth Handloom Census, carried out in 2019-20, counted about 35.2 lakh persons engaged in handloom work.

Within that total are very different kinds of workplace: composite mills, powerloom clusters, handloom weavers, silk, jute and garment factories. Wages and job security differ greatly across them. BMS has also long raised the case of mills run by the National Textile Corporation. A BMS delegation told the Home Minister in June 2025 that 23 NTC mills in eight States had stopped production since the 2020 lockdown, and asked for wage dues to be settled and for 12 selected mills to restart. According to BMS's own report, on 1 September 2026 a delegation that included the general secretaries of the textile and jute federations met the Union Textile Minister for about 75 minutes. A separate post in this series describes that meeting.

## What the three have in common

On the surface, the three industries have little in common. One is run by the State, one is mostly private and fragmented, and one is both. Yet three problems recur:

- **Technology and modernisation.** New machines and new processes change how many people a unit needs, and who gets retrained.
- **Raw materials and imports.** Cotton, wood pulp and other inputs are affected by prices and trade policy, and workers feel the result before anyone else.
- **Changing law.** Since 21 November 2025, the four Labour Codes have replaced 29 earlier central laws. Rules on fixed-term work, contract labour, closure and wages affect every one of these industries.

## BMS's approach

BMS describes its guiding idea as national interest, industry interest and worker interest together. In practice, for these three federations, that means seeking policies that protect jobs while improving the competitiveness of the industry, rather than treating the two aims as opposed. A mill that cannot sell its product cannot pay wages for long, and a worker who is underpaid or unsafe is not a good base for a competitive industry. Whether a given policy meets both tests is something the federations argue over case by case.

## Why it matters to a reader

When BMS announces a demand on behalf of "textile workers" or "paper workers", the first question to ask is which federation is speaking and for whom. The federation names above also help in following press notes and in reading the BMS website, where each federation has its own section. Members who work in one of these industries can find their federation, ask who their local representative is, and put their own questions through it.
